Question:
Form I. Consider the statements

\[ \begin{aligned} (1)\quad&p\land\neg q\land r,\\ (2)\quad&\neg p\land\neg q\land r,\\ (3)\quad&p\land\neg q\land\neg r,\\ (4)\quad&\neg p\land q\land r, \end{aligned} \]

where \(p,\) \(q,\) \(r\) are propositions. How many of these imply the truth of \((p\to q)\to r?\)

Form II. Consider the statements \((1)\) \(p\) and \(r\) are true and \(q\) is false, \((2)\) \(r\) is true and \(p\) and \(q\) are false, \((3)\) \(p\) is true and \(q\) and \(r\) are false, \((4)\) \(q\) and \(r\) are true and \(p\) is false. How many of these imply the truth of the statement “\(r\) is implied by the statement that \(p\) implies \(q\)”?
Solution:
A conditional \(u\to v\) is false only when its hypothesis \(u\) is true and its conclusion \(v\) is false. Apply this rule to the outer conditional \((p\to q)\to r\).

In statements \((1)\), \((2)\), and \((4)\), \(r\) is true. Therefore the outer conditional is true in all three cases, regardless of the truth of \(p\to q\).

In statement \((3)\), \(p\) is true and \(q\) is false, so \(p\to q\) is false. The outer conditional then has a false hypothesis, which makes it true even though \(r\) is false.

The two forms of the question describe the same four truth assignments. All \(\boxed{4}\) make the required statement true, so the answer is \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
